newsitem.title: South africa: Six go free in Malan trial, main player still waits.
newsitem.headline: Six go free in Malan trial, main player still waits.

text.p: Six black South Africans accused of carrying out dirty work for apartheid-era defence minister Magnus Malan were found not guilty on Thursday of massacring 13 civilians.

Malan, the highest-ranking member of the old white government to face trial, will have to wait until Friday to hear his fate when the judge concludes the verdict in the biggest trial of apartheid stalwarts.

Malan and nine other generals and top officials are accused of masterminding a covert divide-and-rule plan to arm Zulu allies for attacks on Nelson Mandela's African National Congress as South Africa sank into violence in the late 1980s.

Their smiles on Thursday may be a sign of growing confidence that they too will go free following the acquittal of the six accused of actually firing the AK-47s that killed 13 children, women and men in KwaMakutha hamlet nine years ago.

The six were members of the police in the KwaZulu homeland run by Mangosuthu Buthelezi, leader of the Inkatha Freedom Party which is the ANC's main black rival. KwaZulu and other homelands were dismantled after South Africa entered all-race democracy in 1994.

Judge Jan Hugo told the Supreme Court in Durban that two key prosecution witnesses -- who helped organise the 1987 bloodbath and testified to try to save their skins -- were liars and the state's case was sloppy.
"Accused numbers one to six have not been proved guilty of the offences charged, they have been acquitted," Hugo said, sparking cries of joy from supporters in the packed court.

The six filed out from their seats in the dock, leaving the balding Malan and grey-haired generals behind. The remaining defendants, who also protest their innocence, will be back in the Edwardian wood-panelled court at 9 a.m. (0700 GMT) on Friday.
"Our boys are out, they are free, they can go home and start their lives again. We are relieved and we thank God," said Koos van der Merwe, a senior Inkatha politician.

Zakhele Khumalo, the party's deputy secretary-general, is the only Inkatha member still on trial but Hugo said prosecutors failed to prove Khumalo knew anything of the bloody attack on the home of the ANC sympathiser who was not even there at the time.
An original 20 defendants were charged with 13 murders, attempted murder and a wider and vaguer charge of conspiracy to murder. Four were freed earlier due to lack of evidence.
Malan, known as accused number 19, sat in a blue suit, taking notes and retaining his well-known stern expression.

Armed forces chief before he joined former president P.W. Botha's cabinet, he is a bogeyman to many blacks who blame him for the violence -- much of it between the ANC and Inkatha -- that brought terror to black townships.

Acquittal would be welcomed by supporters of the old government, who have called the trial a witch hunt. Those who suffered under apartheid say a not-guilty verdict for Malan would be a heavy setback to efforts to punish the crimes of the past.
Malan refuses to apply for amnesty to the "truth commission" where archbishop Desmond Tutu is trying to heal the past, saying he has nothing for which to seek pardon.
During the trial he admitted to helping set up an Inkatha para-military force but said there was nothing sinister about it.
Hugo said it was clear Inkatha para-military trainees had killed the 13 victims. But there was too much doubt about the identity of the killers, commanded by discredited state witness Johan Opperman.
Hugo said the landmark trial would "regrettably" leave unanswered many of the questions it raised.
